newsitem.title: USA: U.S. markets balk at key psychological levels.
newsitem.headline: U.S. markets balk at key psychological levels.

text.p: The U.S. dollar, stocks and Treasuries need confirmation the American economic dream will live on in 1997 before they can resume their bull run through key psychological levels, market watchers said on Friday.
"The rallies are running out of steam," admitted David Resler, chief economist at Nomura Securities International.

Resler said hopes "the American economic dream" of steady growth and low inflation will last drove the 30-year Treasury bond yield near 6.50 percent, the Dow Jones above 7000, and the dollar in the vicinity of 125 yen and 1.70 marks.

U.S. financial instruments have since moved away from these lofty levels set earlier this week. In afternoon trading on Friday, the bond yield was quoted at 6.64 percent, the Dow at 6916 and the dollar at 123.00 yen and 1.6865 marks.

"The markets have bet growth will be moderate, inflation benign while foreign investors will gobble up every U.S. assets in sight," Resler said. "It'll take time for us to get a confirmation of those expectations, if we do get them."
Resler cautioned Treasuries' selloff on good news such as low January inflation data indicated the market has already fully priced in "best-of-both-worlds" expectations.

"I can't identify a likely near-term scenario that would take us convincingly through the 6.50-percent yield," admitted Resler who said it would take signs of a marked economic slowdown to launch a fresh bond rally.

But quantitative analyst Elaine Garzarelli, who heads Garzarelli Capital, expected more good news on the inflation front to fuel a new bond rally that would, in turn, give U.S. equities the scope for a 10- to 15-percent rise.
"Given the inflation rate and the deficit as a share of the Gross Domestic Product, bonds are out of equilibrium with where they should be," Garzarelli said.

"Eventually, the bond market will go back to its equilibrium and bond yields will come down to a level of 6.10 to 6.0 percent and that would fuel a further rally in stocks," predicted Garzarelli, who saw the Dow likely to gain as much as another 1000 points if the low-yield environment materializes.
Such rally in U.S. assets would "be dollar positive," Garzarelli added.

Market players agreed some reassurance from Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan about a steady U.S. interest rate outlook would be crucial. Greenspan is to testify before Congress on the economy and monetary policy on February 26-27.
But William Dudley, chief economist at Goldman, Sachs and Co, viewed it would take more than a steady federal funds rate outlook -- expectations of an easing -- to fuel a bond rally.

"For the bond yield to be stable below 6.50 percent, we would need the perception of an easing," Dudley said. "The flattening of the yield curve can only go so far. You can't buy bonds below 6.50 percent if the funds rate is at 5.25 percent."
Dudley also cautioned the 6.50-percent yield level, usually associated with slow growth, actually reflected the absence of Fed action.
Dudley also pointed out "the yield curve flattening reflects more what the Fed is doing or not doing rather than what the economy is doing."
Goldman, Sachs is forecasting market-adverse developments later this year -- more economic growth and a tightening.
Joe Carson, fixed-income chief economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, expected a 6.0-percent funds rate by yearend.

"It's not Greenspan who is going to determine where the rates will go. Greenspan is watching the econmy and this will determine where the rates go," said Carson who said market players are "are watching the wrong thing."
Carson expected the first U.S. rate hike, when and if it happens, to deal a blow to the bond market, keep the Dow in range but be long-term positive for the dollar.

"Investors are not looking just at the yield but at the rate of return associated with that yield. If the Fed raises rates, investors will pull out to come back when the rates are close to their peak."

Paribas Capital Markets chief economist Brian Fabbri pointed out 6.50 percent is the low end of the current range for the bond yield and that only "suddenly very weak economic news" would allow it to break out of that range.
Fabbri, who expects more economic strength, cautioned "sometimes this year, there'll be a monetary shock" that will negatively affect both stocks and bonds, with mixed implications for the dollar.

Fabbri, however, said a pullback in U.S. equities would be only temporary because "there is a secular move toward higher U.S. stock prices because the baby boomers will continue to save for their retirement."
